rv.q: Gradually, the play reveals itself as a touching celebration of enduring love, family and forgiveness.

For today’s audience, cognisant of what’s to come, it lends an added poignancy to the drama and makes its concerns with ageing, mortality and reconciliation all the more touching. But the tone, for the most part, is comic.
What it needs is a tip-top, fastidious, perfectly pitched production and, with director Emily Burns at the National, this is precisely what it gets.

This glorious revival of Dodie Smith’s interwar family drama is a visual and emotional feast. Director Emily Burns breathes rich life into a weekend gathering to celebrate the golden wedding anniversary of Dora (Lindsay Duncan) and her husband Charles (Malcolm Sinclair).
It is what it is: a slightly soppy, unfashionable play whose 90 years are showing.
Death...form constant motifs but Smith’s gift for comedy keeps us from the abyss.
A gorgeous evening that deserves to spread its tentacles further than this limited run.
Dodie Smith's leisurely play emerges as a real pleasure

cn.t: Dodie Smith's 1938 family drama receives a timely, poignant revival anchored by Lindsay Duncan's superb performance. Critics find the old-fashioned play surprisingly resonant, with its melancholy tone reflecting contemporary anxieties.
